tip: 'Take us to the park' = ले जाते थे (le jate the), literally take-go. Bringing back is ले आना (le aana = take-come). Direction lives in the second verb.
नानी के घर जाते थे (nani ke ghar jate the) = went to grandma's – घर (ghar) needs no word for 'to': 'grandma's home' alone is the destination.
The passive is built on 'go': सुनाई जाती थीं (sunai jati theen) = used to be told, literally 'went being told'. Verb + जाना (jana) = passive.
Hindi flips relative clauses: जिस मकान में हम रहते थे, वह (jis makaan mein hum rahte the, vah) = 'in which house we lived, THAT one'. The closing वह (vah) is required.
No subject at all: पूछते थे (poochhte the) alone means 'people used to ask'. Hindi drops a generic 'people/one' – the verb ending carries it.
'Telling' stories = making them heard: सुनाती थीं (sunati theen) comes from सुनाना (sunana) – सुनना (sunna = hear) + make. Grandma made the stories heard.
Trains walk in Hindi: ट्रेन चलती है (train chalti hai = the train walks). चलना (chalna) covers run, move, work – buses, machines, even watches चलते हैं (chalte hain).
जलेबी मिलती थी (jalebi milti thi) – jalebis 'were gotten', not sold: मिलना (milna) means to be available or received. The same verb also means 'to meet'.
दूधवाला (doodhvala) = the milk one – वाला (vala) sticks to any noun and means 'the one with/of it': सब्ज़ीवाला (sabzivala), रिक्शावाला (rickshavala).
'Came to buy' = ख़रीदने आता था (kharidne aata tha) – purpose takes the -ने (-ne) form of the verb, with no word for 'to' at all.
Villages don't 'have' electricity – Hindi says it 'is in' them: गाँवों में बिजली नहीं होती थी (gaanvon mein bijli nahin hoti thi). There is no verb for 'have'.
उन दिनों (un dinon) = in those days – no में (mein = in) needed. Time phrases in the -ों form work as 'in/during' on their own.
मामा (mama) is only your mother's brother – dad's younger brother is चाचा (chacha), his elder ताऊ (tau). Hindi kinship usually names the side.
Quilts aren't worn, they're draped: रज़ाई ओढ़कर (razai odhkar). ओढ़ना (odhna) covers blankets and shawls; पहनना (pahnna) is for clothes on the body.
गली-गली (gali-gali) = in every single lane – doubling a noun means 'each and every': घर-घर (ghar-ghar) = every house.
Hindi drinks cigarettes: सिगरेट पीते थे (cigarette peete the). पीना (peena) covers both drinking and smoking – there is no separate verb.
खाना खाते थे (khana khate the) = 'ate food' – खाना (khana) is both 'food' and 'to eat', so having a meal doubles it. Perfectly normal Hindi.
हम (hum = we) lands after the verb: पकड़ते थे हम (pakadte the hum) – spoken Hindi tosses known info behind the verb. Neutral order keeps the verb last.
You take fun in Hindi, not have it: तैरने का मज़ा लेते थे (tairne ka maza lete the) = took the fun of swimming. Enjoying = मज़ा लेना (maza lena).
जब हम छोटे थे, तो (jab hum chhote the, to) = 'when we were small, then' – a जब (jab) clause usually opens its main clause with तो (to), which English never translates.
आ जाती तो (aa jaati to) = 'had she come' – the unreal past drops था (tha) entirely. A bare -ती/-ता (-ti/-ta) verb signals 'if only it had happened'.
खा लिया (kha liya) = ate it UP – adding लेना (lena = take) marks an action as fully done. The दीमक (deemak = termites) didn't just eat, they finished the job.
भोर होते ही (bhor hote hi) = the instant dawn broke – verb in -ते (-te) + ही (hi) means 'as soon as'. Works anywhere: आते ही (aate hi) = right on arriving.
Superlatives compare against everyone: सबसे आगे (sabse aage) = 'ahead of all' = furthest ahead. सबसे (sabse) + adjective is how Hindi says '-est'.
कच्चे आम (kachche aam) = raw mangoes – कच्चा (kachcha) is one word for unripe, uncooked, unpaved, half-done. Its opposite पक्का (pakka) covers ripe, cooked, solid.
Position words follow the noun in Hindi: दीवार के पीछे (deewaar ke peechhe) is 'the wall behind' – the reverse of English 'behind the wall'.
बीचोबीच (beechobeech) is बीच (beech = middle) doubled: पुणे के बीचोबीच (Pune ke beechobeech) = right in the center of Pune. Doubling adds the 'exactly'.
Hindi has no verb for 'have'. नरेश के पास (Naresh ke paas) is literally 'near Naresh' – so 'Naresh has 500 rupees' comes out as 'near Naresh are 500 rupees'.
के ऊपर (ke oopar) alone means sitting on top. Motion across adds से (se): पुल के ऊपर से गुज़रती है (pul ke oopar se guzarti hai) = passes over the bridge.
With pronouns, के fuses in: आपके पास (aapke paas) = 'you have' – one word आपके (aapke), never आप के (aap ke). Same fusion in उसके (uske) and इसके (iske).
